meta.title: Who really said "Education Is the Inculcation of the Incomprehensible Into the Ignorant by the Incompetent"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Keynes. The line is first documented in Josiah Stamp's 1933 book Ideals of a Student — in quotation marks, as a saying he quoted and rejected.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Education Is the Inculcation of the Incomprehensible Into the Ignorant by the Incompetent'?
meta.ogDescription: No Keynes source exists. Earliest evidence: Josiah Stamp's Ideals of a Student (1933), quoting it as an existing saying he disagreed with.

answer.label: Not John Maynard Keynes — an anonymous jibe Josiah Stamp quoted in 1933
answer.authorDates: Credited to John Maynard Keynes (1883–1946), English economist — on one hearer’s recollection printed in 1962
answer.sourceLine: Nothing Keynes wrote or published contains this line. The earliest evidence located by Quote Investigator ↗ is Sir Josiah Stamp’s 1933 book Ideals of a Student, where Stamp puts the sentence in quotation marks — signalling it was already in circulation — and then argues against it. The Keynes credit surfaces only in 1962, when Abba Eban recalled hearing it from Keynes at Cambridge in the 1930s.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — no Keynes source exists; the line is first documented as an existing saying that Josiah Stamp quoted in order to reject it.

source.heading: Where the line actually first appears

docMeta.dd: Ideals of a Student, chap. 2, p. 53
Sir Josiah Stamp — who set the sentence in quotation marks and disagreed with it
London: E. Benn, 1933; the preface is dated September 1933, and Stamp says the chapter is based on a commencement address he gave at Toronto that year

source.excerpt: The time has gone by when we can say that education is “the inculcation of the incomprehensible into the ignorant by the incompetent.” Now upon us students is the responsibility: for these complexities of economic life require certain qualities of judgment.
trail: 1933 — The saying surfaces twice in one year, both times around Josiah Stamp: in his book Ideals of a Student, in quotation marks and under protest, and in a “Gleanings” column in The Education Outlook (Spring 1933) crediting him with an “indolent” variant, per Quote Investigator ↗.

1937–1938 — The quotation marks fall away. A Winnipeg paper reports Stamp giving the definition at a school function at Bury St Edmunds in November 1937, and a Greeley, Colorado paper repeats it as his in January 1938 — both cited by Quote Investigator ↗.

1940–1946 — It goes anonymous: “the cynic has it” in a Virginia college periodical in 1940, “some clever modern cynic” in McGill dean Ernest Brown’s January 1942 speech, and a redefinition entry in Great Lakes Technocrat in 1946, all documented in the same investigation ↗.

1962–1979 — Keynes enters, twenty-nine years after the first printings: Abba Eban recalls hearing it from him at Cambridge, and Leo Rosten prints the “indifferent” version under his name in 1979. These are the only two sources Wikiquote can give for it, under “Attributed” ↗.
source.cutTag: Ideals of a Student, chap. 2, p. 53 (1933)
source.excerptNote: Read the punctuation. Stamp quotes the definition rather than coining it, and the sentence around it is a rejection: the time for that view, he says, has gone by. Everything downstream — the newspaper reports, the Keynes credit — strips both the quotation marks and the disagreement.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this sentence: its author is unknown, and the earliest located printing already treats it as an existing saying in circulation. Both 1933 appearances — Stamp’s Ideals of a Student and The Education Outlook — are later than the pre-1931 cutoff that would put a work clearly in the US public domain, and the Internet Archive’s copy of the book is borrow-restricted rather than open, so the surrounding text of that book should be treated as protected.

author.name: Sir Josiah Stamp
author.heading: The man the saying actually stuck to
author.metaLine: 1880–1941 · English economist, statistician & director of the Bank of England
author.bio: Josiah Stamp was, in Wikipedia’s summary, “an English industrialist, economist, civil servant, statistician, writer, and banker” — a director of the Bank of England and chairman of the London, Midland and Scottish Railway, raised to the peerage as Baron Stamp in 1938. He and his wife were killed by a direct hit on the air-raid shelter at their home on 16 April 1941. He is the reason this definition of education spread at all: he used it in speeches through the 1930s and newspapers pinned it to his name — even though he quoted it as someone else’s line and said he disagreed with it.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest evidence located by Quote Investigator: Josiah Stamp, Ideals of a Student (London: E. A second 1933 printing, in “Gleanings,” The Education Outlook 10, no. 1 (Spring 1933): 21, ascribes it to Stamp with “indolent” in place of “ignorant.” The John Maynard Keynes credit traces to Abba Eban, “Israel in the World of Ideas,” Jewish Frontier (October 1962): 3, recalling Keynes at Cambridge in the 1930s. No text by Keynes has been produced.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: Two famous names, one anonymous joke. Neither man is documented as its author — and the one who used it most said he disagreed with it.

items.why: The entire Keynes credit rests on one recollection: in October 1962 the diplomat Abba Eban wrote in Jewish Frontier that he first heard the definition “in Cambridge from Lord Keynes (this was in the ‘thirties).” Leo Rosten repeated the credit in 1979 with “indifferent” swapped in. Quote Investigator calls the linkage weaker and indirect ↗ — plausible as a thing Keynes may have repeated at Cambridge, but no writing of his contains it.

Stamp is where the documented trail starts, and where the name-attachment happened: newspapers in 1937 and 1938 reported him using it in speeches ↗ and simply called it his definition. But in his own 1933 book he set it in quotation marks and wrote that the time for saying it had gone by.

Through the 1940s the saying circulated with no name on it at all — a 1940 Virginia college periodical introduced it as “the cynic has it,” and McGill’s Dean of Engineering Ernest Brown credited only an unnamed modern cynic in a January 1942 speech, per Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.

The middle noun changes with almost every retelling: “indolent” in The Education Outlook (Spring 1933), “ignorant” in the 1937–38 newspaper reports, “indifferent” in Leo Rosten’s 1979 compilation — which is also the form Wikiquote lists as the alternate under “Attributed” ↗. A saying whose wording will not hold still is a saying with no author to fix it.

misattribution.truthLine: The originator is unknown. Quote Investigator’s earliest located evidence ↗ is Josiah Stamp’s Ideals of a Student (1933), and Stamp’s own quotation marks tell you the line was already loose in the world before he picked it up.

context.heading: Why this one travels
lead: It is a perfect piece of engineering: four hard in- words in a row, a whole indictment of schooling in fifteen words, and no verb doing any real work. Alliteration that tight is how a saying survives without a source — it is easier to remember than to check, which is exactly the condition under which quotes drift toward famous names.

And it drifted twice. First to Sir Josiah Stamp, who used it in speeches through the 1930s while explicitly quoting it as somebody else’s — by 1937 a Winnipeg paper had it as Stamp’s own definition delivered at a school function in Bury St Edmunds. Then, decades later, to John Maynard Keynes, on the strength of one man remembering a Cambridge conversation.
context.detailsSummary: The variants, and the strangest citation of all
detailsBody: The middle noun is the unstable part. “Ignorant” is the common form; The Education Outlook printed “indolent” in 1933; Leo Rosten’s 1979 book gave “indifferent”; a 1942 speech by McGill’s Dean of Engineering, Ernest Brown, expanded it to “into the minds of the ignorant” and credited only “some clever modern cynic.”

The oddest turn is in the United States Senate. Testifying on the Public Television Act in April 1967, Westinghouse Broadcasting president Donald McGannon attributed to Keynes not the jibe but a rebuttal of it — calling it a “gross canard” on the grounds that students are far from ignorant. So even the Keynes tradition cannot agree on whether he was making the joke or knocking it down.
context.pull: Stamp put the sentence in quotation marks and then argued against it. The quotation marks did not survive the retelling.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located evidence is Josiah Stamp's 1933 book Ideals of a Student (chap. 2, p. 53, E. Benn, London; preface dated September 1933; chapter based on a commencement address at Toronto that year), where Stamp puts the definition in quotation marks and says the time for saying it has gone by.
QI documents the Spring 1933 'Gleanings' item in The Education Outlook (vol. 10, no. 1, p. 21) ascribing the saying to Sir Josiah Stamp with 'indolent' in place of 'ignorant'.

QI cites a Winnipeg Free Press report of 1 November 1937 that Stamp gave the definition at a school function at Bury St Edmunds, and a Greeley Daily Tribune item of 31 January 1938 repeating it as his.

QI cites a 1940 Hampden-Sydney alumni periodical introducing the line as 'the cynic has it', McGill Dean of Engineering Ernest Brown crediting 'some clever modern cynic' in The Engineering Journal of January 1942, and a 1946 Great Lakes Technocrat redefinition entry.

QI quotes Abba Eban's October 1962 Jewish Frontier article 'Israel in the World of Ideas' (p. 3) saying he first heard the definition 'in Cambridge from Lord Keynes (this was in the thirties)', and states the Keynes linkage is weaker because it appeared decades later and the evidence was indirect.

QI records Westinghouse Broadcasting president Donald McGannon's 27 April 1967 US Senate testimony attributing to Keynes the remark that it is 'a gross canard' to state this definition, and Leo Rosten's 1979 Infinite Riches (p. 165) crediting Keynes with the 'indifferent' variant.

Wikiquote lists 'Education is the inculcation of the incomprehensible into the ignorant by the incompetent' in its Attributed section for John Maynard Keynes, sourced to a hearer's memory in Jewish Frontier vol. 29 (1962), with the alternate 'indifferent' version credited to Leo Calvin Rosten's Infinite Riches (1979), p. 165.
The Internet Archive holds a digitized copy of Sir Josiah Stamp's Ideals of a Student, dated 1933, and the item is access-restricted (borrow-only).

Josiah Stamp, 1st Baron Stamp (born 21 June 1880, died 16 April 1941) was 'an English industrialist, economist, civil servant, statistician, writer, and banker', a director of the Bank of England and chairman of the London, Midland and Scottish Railway; he and his wife were killed by a direct hit on the air-raid shelter at their home on 16 April 1941, and he was raised to the peerage as Baron Stamp in 1938.
John Maynard Keynes was born 5 June 1883 and died 21 April 1946, and is described as an English economist whose writings are the basis of Keynesian economics.

Abba Eban (1915-2002) was a South African-born Israeli diplomat and politician who read Classics and Oriental languages at Queens' College, Cambridge and was a Fellow of Pembroke College from 1938 to 1939.
